before.problem:
The intersection of the planes $3x+6y+3z=0$ and $x-y+2z+3=0$ is given by the line

$$
r(t)=⟨{a}_{1},{a}_{2},0⟩+tb,\,t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).
$$

Calculate ${a}_{1}+{a}_{2},$ and find a possible direction vector $b.$

decision.explanation: At z=0, the plane equations give a₁+2a₂=0 and a₁−a₂=−3. Thus a₂=1 and a₁=−2, so a₁+a₂=−1. The vector ⟨5,−1,−3⟩ is perpendicular to both plane normals: 3(5)+6(−1)+3(−3)=0 and 5−(−1)+2(−3)=0. Therefore option c satisfies both requirements.

after.name: Question 1
after.problem:
The intersection of the planes $3x+6y+3z=0$ and $x-y+2z+3=0$ is given by the line

$$
r(t)=⟨{a}_{1},{a}_{2},0⟩+tb,\,t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).
$$

Calculate ${a}_{1}+{a}_{2},$ and find a possible direction vector $b.$
after.worked_solution:
We're given that there exists a point on the line where $z=0.$ Substituting this into the first equation gives  

$$
3x+6y+3(0)=0\,⟹\,x=-2y,
$$

and substituting $z=0$ and $x=-2y$ into the second equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}x-y+2z+3 & =0 \\ -2y-y+2(0)+3 & =0 \\ -3y & =-3 \\ y & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $x=-2y=-2$ and $a=⟨-2,1,0⟩$ is a position vector of a point on the line.

Next, we notice:

- For the plane $3x+6y+3z=0,$ a normal vector to the plane is ${n}_{1}=⟨3,6,3⟩.$

- For the plane $x-y+2z+3=0,$ a normal vector to the plane is ${n}_{2}=⟨1,-1,2⟩.$

To find a direction vector for the line, we calculate the cross product of these normal vectors:

$$
\begin{aligned}{n}_{1}\times {n}_{2} & =⟨3,6,3⟩\times ⟨1,-1,2⟩ \\  & =\left|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 3 & 6 & 3 \\ 1 & -1 & 2\end{aligned}\right| \\  & =15i-3j-9k \\  & =⟨15,-3,-9⟩\end{aligned}
$$

We can pick any vector that is parallel to ${n}_{1}\times {n}_{2}$ as a direction vector of the line. So, let 

$$
b=\frac{1}{3}({n}_{1}\times {n}_{2})=⟨5,-1,-3⟩.
$$

The equation of the line is:

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =a+tb \\ r(t) & =⟨-2,1,0⟩+t⟨5,-1,-3⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally then, ${a}_{1}+{a}_{2}=-2+1=-1,$ and $b=⟨5,-1,-3⟩.$

r(t)=⟨a1,a2,0⟩+tb,t∈(−∞,∞).

Calculate a1+a2, and find a possible direction vector b.

a
a1+a2=−2,b=⟨5,−1,3⟩
b
a1+a2=1,b=⟨5,1,−3⟩

EXPLANATION

We're given that there exists a point on the line where z=0. Substituting this into the first equation gives

3x+6y+3(0)=0⟹x=−2y,

and substituting z=0 and x=−2y into the second equation gives

x−y+2z+3=0−2y−y+2(0)+3=0−3y=−3y=1.

Therefore, x=−2y=−2 and a=⟨−2,1,0⟩ is a position vector of a point on the line.

Next, we notice:

  • For the plane 3x+6y+3z=0, a normal vector to the plane is n1=⟨3,6,3⟩.

  • For the plane x−y+2z+3=0, a normal vector to the plane is n2=⟨1,−1,2⟩.

To find a direction vector for the line, we calculate the cross product of these normal vectors:

n1×n2=⟨3,6,3⟩×⟨1,−1,2⟩=ijk3631−12=15i−3j−9k=⟨15,−3,−9⟩

We can pick any vector that is parallel to n1×n2 as a direction vector of the line. So, let b=13(n1×n2)=⟨5,−1,−3⟩.

The equation of the line is:

r(t)=a+tbr(t)=⟨−2,1,0⟩+t⟨5,−1,−3⟩

Finally then, a1+a2=−2+1=−1, and b=⟨5,−1,−3⟩.

content.problem:
The intersection of the planes $3x+6y+3z=0$ and $x-y+2z+3=0$ is given by the line

$$
r(t)=⟨{a}_{1},{a}_{2},0⟩+tb,\,t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).
$$

Calculate ${a}_{1}+{a}_{2},$ and find a possible direction vector $b.$
content.worked_solution:
We're given that there exists a point on the line where $z=0.$ Substituting this into the first equation gives  

$$
3x+6y+3(0)=0\,⟹\,x=-2y,
$$

and substituting $z=0$ and $x=-2y$ into the second equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}x-y+2z+3 & =0 \\ -2y-y+2(0)+3 & =0 \\ -3y & =-3 \\ y & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $x=-2y=-2$ and $a=⟨-2,1,0⟩$ is a position vector of a point on the line.

Next, we notice:

- For the plane $3x+6y+3z=0,$ a normal vector to the plane is ${n}_{1}=⟨3,6,3⟩.$

- For the plane $x-y+2z+3=0,$ a normal vector to the plane is ${n}_{2}=⟨1,-1,2⟩.$

To find a direction vector for the line, we calculate the cross product of these normal vectors:

$$
\begin{aligned}{n}_{1}\times {n}_{2} & =⟨3,6,3⟩\times ⟨1,-1,2⟩ \\  & =\left|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 3 & 6 & 3 \\ 1 & -1 & 2\end{aligned}\right| \\  & =15i-3j-9k \\  & =⟨15,-3,-9⟩\end{aligned}
$$

We can pick any vector that is parallel to ${n}_{1}\times {n}_{2}$ as a direction vector of the line. So, let 

$$
b=\frac{1}{3}({n}_{1}\times {n}_{2})=⟨5,-1,-3⟩.
$$

The equation of the line is:

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =a+tb \\ r(t) & =⟨-2,1,0⟩+t⟨5,-1,-3⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally then, ${a}_{1}+{a}_{2}=-2+1=-1,$ and $b=⟨5,-1,-3⟩.$

decision.explanation: Setting y=0 gives a₁−2a₃=8 and 2a₁−3a₃=16. Subtracting twice the first equation from the second yields a₃=0, hence a₁=8 and a₁+a₃=8. The cross product of the normals ⟨1,3,−2⟩ and ⟨2,1,−3⟩ is ⟨−7,−1,−5⟩, a valid direction vector.

after.name: Question 5
after.problem:
The intersection of the planes $x+3y-2z-8=0$ and $2x+y-3z-16=0$ is given by the line

$$
r(t)=⟨{a}_{1},0,{a}_{3}⟩+tb,\,t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).
$$

Calculate ${a}_{1}+{a}_{3},$ and find a possible direction vector $b.$
after.worked_solution:
We're given that there exists a point on the line where $y=0.$ Substituting this into the second equation gives 

$$
x+0-2z-8=0\,⟹\,x=2z+8,
$$

and substituting $y=0$ and $x=2z+8$ into the first equation gives 

$$
\begin{aligned}2(2z+8)+0-3z-16 & =0 \\ 4z+16-3z-16 & =0 \\ z & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $x=2(0)+8=8$ and $a=⟨8,0,0⟩$ is a position vector of a point on the line.

Next, we notice:

- For the plane $x+3y-2z-8=0,$ a normal vector to the plane is ${n}_{1}=⟨1,3,-2⟩.$

- For the plane $2x+y-3z-16=0,$ a normal vector to the plane is ${n}_{2}=⟨2,1,-3⟩.$

To find a direction vector for the line, we calculate the cross product of these normal vectors:

$$
\begin{aligned}{n}_{1}\times {n}_{2} & =⟨1,3,-2⟩\times ⟨2,1,-3⟩ \\  & =\left|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 1 & 3 & -2 \\ 2 & 1 & -3\end{aligned}\right| \\  & =-7i-j-5k \\  & =⟨-7,-1,-5⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the equation of the line is:

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =a+tb \\ r(t) & =⟨8,0,0⟩+t⟨-7,-1,-5⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally then, ${a}_{1}+{a}_{3}=8+0=8,$ and $b=⟨-7,-1,-5⟩.$

$$
x+0-2z-8=0\,⟹\,x=2z+8,
$$

and substituting $y=0$ and $x=2z+8$ into the first equation gives 

$$
\begin{aligned}2(2z+8)+0-3z-16 & =0 \\ 4z+16-3z-16 & =0 \\ z & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $x=2(0)+8=8$ and $a=⟨8,0,0⟩$ is a position vector of a point on the line.

Next, we notice:

- For the plane $x+3y-2z-8=0,$ a normal vector to the plane is ${n}_{1}=⟨1,3,-2⟩.$

- For the plane $2x+y-3z-16=0,$ a normal vector to the plane is ${n}_{2}=⟨2,1,-3⟩.$

To find a direction vector for the line, we calculate the cross product of these normal vectors:

$$
\begin{aligned}{n}_{1}\times {n}_{2} & =⟨1,3,-2⟩\times ⟨2,1,-3⟩ \\  & =\left|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 1 & 3 & -2 \\ 2 & 1 & -3\end{aligned}\right| \\  & =-7i-j-5k \\  & =⟨-7,-1,-5⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the equation of the line is:

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =a+tb \\ r(t) & =⟨8,0,0⟩+t⟨-7,-1,-5⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally then, ${a}_{1}+{a}_{3}=8+0=8,$ and $b=⟨-7,-1,-5⟩.$
